question: A junior risk analyst at a Swiss private bank is presenting the Sharpe ratio to newly hired analysts, in the context of clients who place their entire risky wealth in a single actively managed CHF portfolio. Which of the following statements in the presentation is most accurate?

options.A: The Sharpe ratio divides the portfolio’s average excess return by its beta, so it measures the reward earned per unit of the systematic risk borne by the client.
options.B: The Sharpe ratio is the relevant measure when the portfolio is one of many subportfolios combined into a larger fund, because each subportfolio’s nonsystematic risk is then retained in full.
options.C: Because a client can always choose a passive indexed equity fund instead, an active portfolio held as the entire risky portfolio must offer a higher Sharpe ratio than the market index to be an acceptable candidate.
options.D: Moving part of the portfolio into T-bills raises its Sharpe ratio, because mixing with the risk-free asset lowers volatility by proportionally more than it lowers excess return.

solution:
Junior analyst at a Swiss private bank presents the Sharpe ratio for clients holding one active portfolio as their entire risky wealth.

**Concept and theory**

The Sharpe ratio is the oldest reward-to-volatility measure. GARP defines it as

$\text{S}_{\text{P}} = \frac{\bar{r}_{\text{P}} - \bar{r}_{\text{f}}}{\sigma_{\text{P}}}$ ,

where $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{P}}$ is the average portfolio return over the sample, $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}}$ the average risk-free rate (a sample average because the rate may move), and $\sigma_{\text{P}}$ the standard deviation of portfolio returns over the same period. The numerator is the reward for bearing risk; the denominator is total risk, systematic plus nonsystematic.

question:
The CIO of a Canadian public pension plan must choose a performance measure for each of three decisions:

I. Selecting one balanced fund that will hold the entire risky allocation of a small supplementary plan.

II. Ranking twelve external equity managers, each of which will run one sleeve of the main plan’s multi-manager risky portfolio.

III. Selecting a hedge fund to add as an active position alongside the main plan’s largely passive, indexed equity core.

Which assignment of measures to decisions I, II and III, respectively, is most appropriate?

options.A: Sharpe ratio; Treynor measure; information ratio.
options.B: Treynor measure; Sharpe ratio; information ratio.
options.C: Sharpe ratio; information ratio; Treynor measure.
options.D: Sharpe ratio; Treynor measure; Jensen’s alpha.

solution:
Canadian pension CIO assigns a measure to three decisions: entire risky fund, one sleeve of many, hedge fund added to indexed core.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s central message for this LO is that “the appropriate performance measure depends on the role of the portfolio to be evaluated”. Each measure uses the risk that actually matters to the investor in that role.

- **Entire investment fund.** All of the portfolio’s volatility is borne; nothing else diversifies it. Use the Sharpe ratio, ($\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{P}} -$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}} )$/$\sigma_{\text{P}}$.
- **One subportfolio of many.** When a sponsor such as CalPERS parcels assets out to many managers, each manager’s nonsystematic risk is largely diversified away across the managers, “so only systematic risk is relevant”. […]

options.B: Like the Sharpe ratio, Jensen’s alpha penalizes nonsystematic risk, so a poorly diversified portfolio will show a lower alpha than an otherwise identical well-diversified portfolio.
options.C: Any positive estimated alpha identifies a superior manager, regardless of the statistical significance of the estimate or the length of the sample period.

question: A risk consultant reviewing a UK pension scheme’s manager report notices that one GBP equity fund ranks 2nd of 8 peer funds on the Treynor measure but 7th of 8 on the Sharpe ratio, over the same period and with the same risk-free rate. Which conclusion should the consultant draw?

options.A: The fund’s beta must have been mismeasured, because the two measures share the same numerator and therefore always rank funds identically.
options.B: The fund carries substantial unsystematic risk relative to its peers; the rank gap signals poor diversification, although it is not an absolute measure of how undiversified the fund is.
options.C: The fund is better diversified than its peers, because diversifiable risk lowers a fund’s Treynor measure while leaving its Sharpe ratio unaffected.

solution:
UK consultant sees a fund rank 2nd on Treynor but 7th on Sharpe among eight peers.

Sharpe and Treynor share the same numerator, average excess return over the risk-free rate. They differ only in the risk denominator: total SD for Sharpe, beta for Treynor. Total risk equals systematic plus unsystematic risk. For a well-diversified portfolio unsystematic risk is small, total and systematic risk are close, and the two measures rank portfolios almost identically. Schweser: for a less well-diversified portfolio, “the difference in rankings based on the two measures is likely due to the amount of diversification”. question: A board member of a UK charity is reviewing a consultant’s report. Over three years, the charity’s high-yield bond manager had the 8th-best return among 80 funds in the consultant’s high-yield comparison universe, and the consultant calls this “90th percentile performance, clearly justifying the fees”. Which criticism of the consultant’s conclusion is most valid?

options.A: The universe median is not an investable strategy, so the ranking does not show whether the manager beat what a passive investor could have earned, and durations may differ across funds in the universe.
options.B: The ranking ignores investment style, because comparison universes pool all fixed-income funds together regardless of their credit quality or risk characteristics.

UK charity board member reviews a consultant’s “90th percentile” universe ranking of a high-yield manager.

Funds are grouped into comparison universes (high-yield bonds, growth equity and so on); their (usually time-weighted) average returns are ordered and each manager gets a percentile rank. The ninth-best of 100 is the 90th percentile manager: better than 90% of competitors.

**Concept and theory**

Sharpe’s style analysis is a constrained regression. The coefficients are meant to be read as the fund’s effective asset allocation, so they must look like a real allocation of a long-only fund: each between zero and one and together summing to one. GARP gives the reason explicitly: “Because funds are barred from short positions, the regression coefficients are constrained to be either zero or positive and to sum to 100%.” Only under both constraints do the coefficients form a complete allocation that can be used to build a passive tracking portfolio.

question: The CRO of a Canadian public sector pension plan is presenting the style analysis of an external CAD equity manager to the investment committee. The regression R-square is 99%. One committee member argues: “With an R-square of 99%, the manager’s stock picking clearly contributes nothing, so we should replace the mandate with a passive mix of the style indexes.” Which response by the CRO is most accurate?

options.A: The R-square measures only the share of return variability explained by style; the intercept, which measures the average return from security selection, can be positive even with an R-square of 100%, so it must be examined first.
options.B: The member is right, because with an R-square of 99% at most 1% of the manager’s average return can have come from security selection, which is too little to justify active fees.
options.C: The member is wrong, because the 1% of variability that style does not explain is itself the manager’s annual return from security selection, so the manager adds about 1% per year.
options.D: The member is wrong, because in Sharpe’s method the share of return variability attributable to style is measured by the sum of the coefficients, which is always 100%, not by the R-square.

solution:
Canadian pension CRO: responding to the claim that R-square 99% means stock picking adds nothing.

**Concept and theory**

R-square and intercept answer different questions. R-square tells you how much of the variability of returns moves with the style indexes. The intercept tells you the average level of return earned on top of the style mix, which GARP calls the average return from security selection. A manager can track the style mix very closely month to month (R-square near 100%) while beating it by a steady margin every month (positive intercept). question:
A portfolio manager at a Zurich private bank is reviewing a CHF-hedged fund marketed to clients as a “small-cap value” fund. She runs Sharpe’s style analysis on seven style portfolios and obtains the following output.

| Style portfolio | Coeff. (%) | Style portfolio | Coeff. (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| T-bill | 0 | High P/E (growth) | 16 |
| Small cap | 4 | Medium P/E | 0 |
| Medium cap | 22 | Low P/E (value) | 0 |
| Large cap | 58 | R-square | 95 |

Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.A: The fund is consistent with its small-cap value label, because an R-square of 95% shows that its returns are well explained by the style portfolios.
options.B: The fund’s effective style is mainly large cap with some medium cap and a growth tilt, which is inconsistent with its small-cap value label.
options.C: The fund’s style cannot be inferred, because Sharpe’s method requires a positive coefficient on every style portfolio included in the regression.
options.D: The fund’s label must be taken as its style, because style analysis estimates only the fund’s market beta and not its exposures to size or growth segments.

solution:
Zurich PM: what the coefficients say about a fund labelled small-cap value.

**Concept and theory**

Because the coefficients are effective allocations to style portfolios, they reveal the manager’s investment style regardless of the label. Schweser’s step 3: the regression slopes are used to infer the investment style of the manager. GARP’s Magellan example shows the reading: of seven style portfolios only large cap (61), medium cap (35) and high P/E growth (5) had positive coefficients, so “the fund returns are well represented by three style portfolios”. Zero coefficients are normal: a fund need not load on every style. The R-square says how well the chosen mix describes the fund, not which mix it is.
